title: GPU fleet provisioning sync w/ AWS (time-to-ready blockers)
summary: Redwood walked through current Dedicated fleet bring-up path and where "allocated -> joined -> validating -> ready" is stalling in us-east A100 pools. AWS team dug into suspected causes: EFA/placement group behavior, ENA/SR-IOV timing, IMDSv2 + cloud-init delays, and VPC egress constraints during golden image bootstrapping. Agreed on a short set of experiments (EFA attach timing, IMDS hop limit, VPC endpoints for S3/ECR, and per-AZ IP capacity checks) and on what logs/instance metadata Redwood should capture during failures. Ended with action items and next sync scheduling.
topics: Baseline time-to-ready and where delays concentrate (boot, kube join, validation)
Golden AMI baking vs first-boot installs (NVIDIA drivers/CUDA/NCCL)
EFA enablement and placement group constraints for A100 capacity
Networking quirks: CNI, security groups, NACLs, VPC endpoints, IP exhaustion
Instance metadata service (IMDSv2) impact on cloud-init and node agent
Recommendations for instrumentation and AWS support escalation paths
questions: Does EFA attach and placement group creation add measurable latency or intermittent failures for new capacity in us-east-1?
Can we avoid first-boot driver installs entirely by pinning to a baked AMI and using Nitro Enclaves/IMDS settings safely?
Are there known issues with ENA/SR-IOV readiness that cause early NCCL all-reduce flakes within the first ~10 minutes after boot?
What are best practices for minimizing dependency on public egress during provisioning (S3/ECR endpoints)?
Which CloudWatch/EC2 signals are most useful for correlating instance bring-up problems with underlying hardware events?
next_steps: Redwood to share a small bundle of failing-instance artifacts (cloud-init logs, dmesg, EFA/ENA status, kubelet logs) from two recent us-east A100 failures.
AWS to confirm current recommended AMI + driver baseline for A100 (and any known issues with recent NVIDIA driver versions on that instance family).
AWS to advise on EFA + placement group configuration and whether we should move to a specific strategy (cluster vs spread) for bring-up reliability.
Redwood to test provisioning with S3 + ECR VPC endpoints enabled (no public egress) and compare time-to-ready P50/P95.
Schedule follow-up sync for the week of 2025-10-22 after Redwood runs 2–3 controlled bring-up batches.
action_items: Redwood (Sahana) - Export current AMI bake pipeline step list and where first-boot installs still occur; include exact driver/CUDA/NCCL versions and timestamps from last 5 bakes - Due 2025-10-17

Redwood (Gabe) - Capture and share cloud-init-output.log, /var/log/messages (or journald), kubelet logs, and validation agent logs from one node that gets stuck in Validating > 30 min - Due 2025-10-17
AWS (Arjun) - Send reference for IMDSv2 settings (hop limit, token TTL) and known cloud-init impacts; recommend safe defaults for kube node bootstrap - Due 2025-10-18

AWS (Derek) - Check for any recent A100 host-level advisories in us-east-1 related to EFA/ENA initialization or PCIe training delays; confirm what support case details would be most helpful - Due 2025-10-18
AWS (Priya K.) - Review Redwood VPC layout assumptions: NAT/egress, route tables, NACLs, and IP capacity per subnet/AZ; flag any likely IP exhaustion or ephemeral port constraints - Due 2025-10-21
Redwood (Harish) - Run one controlled bring-up batch with EFA disabled to isolate network fabric vs software causes; report deltas in time-to-ready and validation pass rate - Due 2025-10-22
Redwood (Vanessa) - Draft short problem statement + metrics for potential AWS escalation (time-to-ready regression, failure modes, impacted AZs) - Due 2025-10-22
transcript:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Title: GPU fleet provisioning sync w/ AWS (time-to-ready blockers)
Date: 2025-10-15
Time: 17:00 - 17:52 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees:
- Redwood Inference: Jamal Pierce, Vanessa Ortiz, Sahana Iyer, Harish Reddy, Gabe Wilson
- AWS: Megan R. (TAM), Arjun S. (Solutions Architect), Derek L. (EC2 Specialist SA), Priya K. (Networking Specialist)

Auto-Generated Notes (may be incomplete)
Summary: Discussed delays in GPU node provisioning and readiness gating; reviewed AMI baking constraints, EFA/placement group setup, and VPC egress/IP capacity. Agreed on experiments and log collection for follow-up.

---

[00:00] Megan (AWS TAM): Alright, we’re recording. Thanks everyone. Goal today is to understand the instance bring-up failures you’re seeing, especially for the A100 capacity, and what we can do from our side. Jamal, do you want to kick us off with a quick overview?

[00:18] Jamal (Redwood): Yep, thanks Megan. So, context: we’re in a sprint to automate “provision-to-ready” for GPU nodes. For our Dedicated pools we’re trying to get allocated to ready without humans. Right now, us-east A100 is the first staged rollout and it’s… it’s not terrible but it’s not stable enough. We get nodes stuck before they’re ready, mostly in what we call validating.

[00:42] Vanessa (Redwood): And the time-to-ready tail is long. Median is okay, the P95 is the problem. We’ll have some nodes come up in, say, 18–25 minutes, and then others are 60+ minutes or fail and get reimaged. That kills our capacity predictability.

[01:02] Arjun (AWS SA): When you say “validating,” what’s happening there? Is that Kubernetes join, or post-join tests?

[01:08] Gabe (Redwood): Post-join. So the sequence is like: instance allocated, boot, cloud-init runs, we do some bootstrap, then kubelet joins cluster. After that, a daemonset runs checks: GPU health, driver parity, networking throughput, and an NCCL all-reduce smoke. If those pass, we mark it Ready and it can join serving.

[01:31] Derek (AWS EC2 Specialist): What’s the main failure signature? Is it EFA init, NCCL failures, or timeouts waiting for the device plugin?

[01:39] Harish (Redwood): It’s a mix. Some are kubelet never joins because bootstrap hangs on pulling artifacts. That seems like network/egress. Some are NCCL smoke flakes, which could be fabric or just early jitter. And a smaller bucket is driver mismatch, like the node comes up but the driver version doesn’t match what the pool expects.

[02:03] Sahana (Redwood): On that last one, we’re actively trying to eliminate first-boot driver installs. We bake AMIs, but there are still pieces that run at boot: a small verification and sometimes a reinstall if the install didn’t finish cleanly. That’s part of what we want to stop doing.

[02:22] Megan (AWS TAM): Got it. So three buckets: bootstrap dependency on external downloads, K8s join, and post-join performance checks. Priya, I think the egress and endpoints part is you.

[02:32] Priya K. (AWS Networking): Yeah. First question: do these subnets have NAT egress, or are you using VPC endpoints for S3, ECR, etc.?

[02:41] Harish (Redwood): Today it’s mostly NAT for outbound, and we’re not fully on endpoints. We do have private ECR access in some places but not consistent.

[02:50] Priya K. (AWS Networking): That’s a common source of tail latency, especially if you’re pulling drivers or packages from public repos at boot. Even if it’s “fast,” NAT is a shared dependency. Also check ephemeral port exhaustion on the NAT gateway if you’re bringing up a batch.

[03:07] Vanessa (Redwood): Yeah, we tend to bring up in batches. Not huge, like 8–32 nodes, but enough to stampede.

[03:16] Arjun (AWS SA): If you can move those pulls to S3 and use a gateway endpoint, that often reduces variability. Also, if cloud-init is waiting on metadata calls and IMDS is slow or blocked, you get weird hangs.

[03:32] Gabe (Redwood): We do IMDSv2, and I know we changed some settings recently. Could that actually add seconds-to-minutes?

[03:40] Arjun (AWS SA): It can, if token retrieval is being retried, or hop limit is wrong in containerized contexts. Also if you have something in bootstrap using IMDS from within a container without host networking, sometimes it’s not reachable depending on iptables rules.

[03:56] Sahana (Redwood): Our validation agent runs as a daemonset and does call metadata for instance ID and AZ. That’s after join, but it could be failing.

[04:07] Derek (AWS EC2 Specialist): For A100 specifically, are these p4d or p4de? Or…

[04:12] Harish (Redwood): Primarily p4d right now.

[04:15] Derek (AWS EC2 Specialist): Okay. Then EFA is in play if you’re using it. Are you enabling EFA at launch?

[04:22] Vanessa (Redwood): We are for the Dedicated pools. The NCCL smoke test assumes EFA path is correct; we want to catch fabric issues early.

[04:32] Derek (AWS EC2 Specialist): EFA attach should be pretty fast, but placement group constraints can cause odd behavior. Are you launching into a placement group? Cluster placement group, I assume?

[04:41] Harish (Redwood): Yes, cluster placement group.

[04:43] Derek (AWS EC2 Specialist): For bring-up, cluster placement group is good for performance, but it’s more strict. If capacity is fragmented in the AZ, you’ll see slower fulfillment and sometimes instances land differently than expected if the request is modified. Are you seeing allocation delays, or just post-boot?

[04:59] Jamal (Redwood): Allocation is mostly fine. It’s after instance is “running” that the timer stretches.

[05:07] Megan (AWS TAM): That points more to bootstrap and network rather than EC2 capacity fulfillment.

[05:13] Vanessa (Redwood): I’ll add one more weirdness: we saw some nodes where `nvidia-smi` is fine, but the first NCCL test fails, and then five minutes later it passes if we rerun. We’re trying to decide whether to add warmup or tune timeouts.

[05:29] Derek (AWS EC2 Specialist): That can happen if the network interface or EFA stack isn’t fully settled or if your test is too aggressive right after boot. Also, you might want to confirm that the EFA installer/kernel module is in the AMI and not being installed on boot.

[05:44] Sahana (Redwood): It’s in the AMI, but we run a service that verifies versions. I can confirm the exact packages.

[05:51] Priya K. (AWS Networking): Also, if you’re doing any CNI changes or MTU changes on boot, it can cause transient packet loss. Are you setting MTU for EFA / jumbo frames?

[06:01] Gabe (Redwood): We set MTU in a node config baseline. It’s supposed to be consistent, but I’m not 100% sure it’s applied before the NCCL test.

[06:10] Vanessa (Redwood): Our gating order is: GPU health and driver parity, then network throughput, then NCCL. But we’ve debated moving network checks earlier.

[06:21] Arjun (AWS SA): That order is okay, but you may want a small “network readiness” check before the heavy test. Something like verifying interface is up, correct MTU, routes, and that EFA device is present.

[06:33] Harish (Redwood): We do check `fi_info` and presence of `/dev/infiniband`… well for EFA it’s not infiniband, but you know what I mean. The transcript will probably say “infinite band.”

[06:44] (crosstalk)

[06:45] Megan (AWS TAM): No worries. Fireflies will do its best.

[06:49] Jamal (Redwood): On the image side: we want to standardize golden AMIs with pinned drivers, CUDA minor, NCCL. The question is: is there any constraint we should know about for baking AMIs for p4d and then using them across regions?

[07:04] Derek (AWS EC2 Specialist): Not a hard constraint, but you want to use the right base OS and ensure kernel compatibility with the NVIDIA driver. Also keep in mind that if you’re using EFA, the EFA installer is tied to kernel versions. So if you upgrade kernel, you need to update EFA packages and probably test.

[07:21] Sahana (Redwood): Yeah, we’ve had “driver install mismatch” during image bake. It’s usually when a repo changes or a dependency fails. We’re pinning more aggressively now.

[07:33] Arjun (AWS SA): Are you using the AWS Deep Learning AMI as a base, or your own minimal OS?

[07:38] Sahana (Redwood): Our own hardened Ubuntu base. Security wants tight control; we can’t just take DLAMI as-is.

[07:46] Megan (AWS TAM): Understood.

[07:49] Priya K. (AWS Networking): For the “pull artifacts” part: what are you pulling at boot?

[07:55] Gabe (Redwood): Container images mostly. Validation agent, some internal tooling, and a perf canary image. We use ECR for most of it, plus a couple files from S3.

[08:07] Priya K. (AWS Networking): If ECR is behind NAT and you have a burst of nodes, token fetch + layer pulls can be variable. VPC interface endpoints for ECR API and ECR DKR plus S3 gateway endpoint helps a lot.

[08:22] Vanessa (Redwood): Is there any gotcha with interface endpoints and DNS that could slow down bootstrap? Like if you misconfigure private DNS?

[08:29] Priya K. (AWS Networking): Yes. If private DNS is on and you have split-horizon issues, it can look like “random timeouts.” But generally it’s stable once set. We can review the VPC settings if you share.

[08:41] Jamal (Redwood): We can share sanitized VPC layout and the Terraform module outputs, sure.

[08:47] Megan (AWS TAM): Great.

[08:49] Derek (AWS EC2 Specialist): On the NCCL smoke test: what are the timeouts? And how many GPUs are you testing across?

[08:56] Vanessa (Redwood): Right now it’s a small multi-node all-reduce. It’s not the full training scale, but it is cross-node. Timeout is 180 seconds for the test, and we allow two retries.

[09:10] Derek (AWS EC2 Specialist): If it’s right after boot, you might extend timeout or add a short delay before the first attempt. Also check that the security group allows the necessary traffic between nodes for EFA. Sometimes people forget ephemeral ports.

[09:24] Priya K. (AWS Networking): EFA uses UDP-based traffic patterns; you need wide intra-SG allowances. If you have restrictive NACLs, that can cause flakiness.

[09:35] Harish (Redwood): Our SG is basically “allow all within the node group,” but I’ll confirm NACL.

[09:43] Gabe (Redwood): We had one case where kubelet joined, but the CNI plugin took a long time to become ready. That delayed the daemonset checks. So “Validating” was really “waiting for pods.”

[09:56] Arjun (AWS SA): That’s actually common. If your CNI depends on pulling images and those pulls are slow, it becomes circular. Endpoints can help. Also, consider pre-pulling critical images in the AMI or via a systemd unit before kubelet marks ready.

[10:13] Sahana (Redwood): We’ve considered pre-pull, but it can blow up image size and complicate patch cadence.

[10:20] Vanessa (Redwood): We want the provisioning system to be deterministic and auditable. Pre-pull helps but feels like a band-aid.

[10:28] Megan (AWS TAM): Let’s anchor on what we can do quickly versus longer-term.

[10:33] Jamal (Redwood): Quick wins: reduce dependency on public egress, confirm IMDS settings, and tune NCCL smoke to reduce false quarantines.

[10:43] Derek (AWS EC2 Specialist): About quarantine: when does your system decide to quarantine vs retry?

[10:47] Gabe (Redwood): After repeated validation failures, we quarantine. Quarantined nodes don’t join serving pools. It’s safer, but if we quarantine too aggressively we can cause a capacity shortfall.

[11:01] Vanessa (Redwood): Exactly. We had an internal escalation where too many nodes quarantined and the pool throughput dipped.

[11:07] Megan (AWS TAM): So we want to reduce flakes and distinguish “real hardware/network issue” from “boot jitter.”

[11:15] Derek (AWS EC2 Specialist): For hardware events, you can look at system logs for Xid errors. Also EC2 has instance status checks, but GPU-level issues won’t always show up there. If you collect dmesg and nvidia logs, support can correlate.

[11:31] Arjun (AWS SA): Also, confirm that your kernel parameters and IRQ settings aren’t interfering. But that’s more on your baseline standard.

[11:39] Sahana (Redwood): Our baseline includes a bunch of sysctls and ulimits. We can share the subset relevant to network and metadata.

[11:47] Priya K. (AWS Networking): Another thing: IP capacity in your subnets. If you’re using prefix delegation or have a lot of pods per node, you can run out of IPs and the CNI will be unhappy, delaying readiness.

[12:01] Gabe (Redwood): We’re not at super high pod density on these nodes, but during validation we do spin up some pods.

[12:09] Vanessa (Redwood): Still a good call-out. We should check per-AZ headroom and not just overall.

[12:16] Megan (AWS TAM): Can you share which AZs are impacted most?

[12:20] Harish (Redwood): Mainly us-east-1a and 1c. But not exclusively.

[12:26] Derek (AWS EC2 Specialist): Noted.

[12:29] (brief pause)

[12:31] Jamal (Redwood): Let’s talk about IMDS. We set IMDSv2 required. We might have changed hop limit. Arjun, what do you recommend?

[12:41] Arjun (AWS SA): Typically hop limit 2 is safe for most setups, but if you’re calling IMDS from within containers you need to consider the path. If you set hop limit to 1 and there’s any forwarding, it breaks. Also ensure your bootstrap script is handling token fetch failures gracefully.

[13:00] Gabe (Redwood): We do a retry loop, but the backoff might be too aggressive and block boot.

[13:07] Vanessa (Redwood): We’ve seen “cloud-init waiting for network” and it’s unclear if it’s really network or metadata.

[13:14] Priya K. (AWS Networking): Cloud-init can be misleading. It may be waiting for DNS resolution or reaching a URL.

[13:22] Sahana (Redwood): We can provide cloud-init-output logs for a stuck node.

[13:27] Megan (AWS TAM): Yes, that would help.

[13:31] Derek (AWS EC2 Specialist): On EFA: are you using the EFA-enabled AMI components? There’s a package set. If you have mismatched versions, you can see intermittent failure.

[13:42] Sahana (Redwood): We use the EFA installer packages pinned, but we might have an OS kernel update in the pipeline.

[13:49] Derek (AWS EC2 Specialist): Then you definitely need to re-validate EFA module. Otherwise it might build at boot, which is slow.

[13:58] Vanessa (Redwood): That resonates. We want “no compiling at boot.”

[14:03] Arjun (AWS SA): Another angle: if you’re using bottlerocket or AL2 it’s different, but you said Ubuntu.

[14:09] Sahana (Redwood): Yes.

[14:11] Jamal (Redwood): Okay. Experiment proposal: bring up a batch with EFA disabled, just to see if the NCCL smoke failures disappear.

[14:20] Derek (AWS EC2 Specialist): That’s a good isolation test. You may still want a basic network check, but you can avoid EFA complexities.

[14:28] Vanessa (Redwood): Our inference workloads don’t require EFA the same way training does, but for multi-GPU nodes we still care about networking stability. EFA is mainly for the fabric tests and future-proofing.

[14:42] Priya K. (AWS Networking): If inference traffic is mostly north-south and not heavy east-west, you might not need EFA for serving. But if your validation uses it, it becomes a gate.

[14:52] Gabe (Redwood): Right.

[14:55] Megan (AWS TAM): Also, if you decide not to use EFA for the first stage, that could stabilize time-to-ready while you iterate.

[15:03] Vanessa (Redwood): We’ll consider it, but we don’t want to paper over a real networking issue. If it’s a misconfig, better to fix.

[15:12] Arjun (AWS SA): Agree.

[15:14] (crosstalk)

[15:16] Jamal (Redwood): Let’s shift to the AMI baking constraints. Our bake pipeline runs in CI, and we promote candidate to stable based on validation pass rate. Are there known AWS service limits that could affect baking or launching with new AMIs?

[15:32] Megan (AWS TAM): AMI launch shouldn’t be limited beyond normal account limits. But if you’re copying AMIs across regions, that takes time and can be rate-limited. Also ensure you’re not hitting API throttling during large fleet launches.

[15:46] Gabe (Redwood): We do see some throttling on Describe calls when we launch batches.

[15:51] Megan (AWS TAM): We can look at your API request rates. But your main symptom is post-boot, so focus there first.

[16:00] Priya K. (AWS Networking): When nodes pull from ECR, they also hit STS. If STS is only public and you have strict egress, it can fail. There’s a VPC endpoint for STS too.

[16:14] Harish (Redwood): We don’t have STS endpoint today.

[16:17] Priya K. (AWS Networking): That’s another quick win.

[16:21] Vanessa (Redwood): Noted.

[16:23] Derek (AWS EC2 Specialist): For the GPU health checks: are you checking ECC, Xid codes, that sort of thing?

[16:30] Gabe (Redwood): Yes. We parse `nvidia-smi -q` and kernel logs. We quarantine on certain Xid codes and high ECC counts.

[16:39] Derek (AWS EC2 Specialist): Good. If you can share the specific Xid codes you’re seeing, we can correlate with known issues.

[16:48] Vanessa (Redwood): We’ve seen a couple, but not consistent. Most failures aren’t GPU errors; they’re “NCCL timeout” or “network throughput below threshold.”

[16:59] Priya K. (AWS Networking): That could be noisy early in boot. Throughput tests can fail if the instance is still doing background tasks.

[17:07] Sahana (Redwood): Like apt updates. Which we try to disable, but sometimes it sneaks back.

[17:13] Arjun (AWS SA): Another reason to bake and lock it down.

[17:18] Jamal (Redwood): Yep.

[17:20] Megan (AWS TAM): Let’s get concrete. What artifacts can you share after this call?

[17:26] Gabe (Redwood): From a stuck node: cloud-init-output.log, dmesg, kubelet logs, containerd logs, and our validation agent logs. Also EFA status output.

[17:37] Vanessa (Redwood): Plus timeline timestamps: when instance enters running, when it joins cluster, and when each validation step starts.

[17:46] Megan (AWS TAM): Perfect.

[17:49] Priya K. (AWS Networking): If you can also share the subnet IDs or at least the IP ranges and how many instances you’re bringing up per subnet, I can sanity check IP capacity.

[18:00] Harish (Redwood): We can do that in a sanitized way.

[18:03] Derek (AWS EC2 Specialist): And for the NCCL flakes: can you share what command you run? And whether it uses EFA or TCP.

[18:11] Vanessa (Redwood): We can share a snippet. It uses NCCL tests with env vars to prefer EFA, yes.

[18:18] Derek (AWS EC2 Specialist): Great.

[18:20] (pause)

[18:22] Jamal (Redwood): One thing we heard: sometimes ENA or SR-IOV isn’t fully ready immediately. Is there a recommended wait or check before running network tests?

[18:33] Priya K. (AWS Networking): You can check interface link state and maybe verify `ethtool` reports expected speed. For EFA, there’s `fi_info` and EFA metrics. But a simple approach is a short backoff with jitter before the heavy test.

[18:48] Vanessa (Redwood): That’s what we’re leaning toward.

[18:51] Arjun (AWS SA): Also, avoid doing too much concurrently at first boot. If cloud-init is doing package installs and kubelet is pulling images and your validation is running, you’re saturating disk and network simultaneously.

[19:05] Sahana (Redwood): We’re trying to sequence it better in the orchestrator.

[19:10] Gabe (Redwood): Our orchestrator has retries per step; we can adjust ordering so validation only starts after certain services are stable.

[19:20] Megan (AWS TAM): That sounds like a good plan.

[19:23] Jamal (Redwood): On time-to-ready: our target is to bring P95 under 35 minutes for this pool. Right now it’s closer to… 55, and success rate is in the low 90s. We need high 98+.

[19:39] Megan (AWS TAM): Understood. We can help you isolate the AWS-managed factors.

[19:44] Derek (AWS EC2 Specialist): For anything that looks like underlying host issues, opening a support case with instance IDs and timestamps is the best path. But you need to capture those IDs.

[19:54] Gabe (Redwood): We have them. Our readiness service stores instance IDs and state transitions.

[20:00] Arjun (AWS SA): Good.

[20:02] (minor transcription glitch)

[20:03] Vanessa (Redwood): Another question: does cluster placement group have any documented impact on network stability during early boot?

[20:11] Derek (AWS EC2 Specialist): Not specifically “early boot,” but it constrains where you can land. If the group is full or fragmented, you might see partial placement and then your cross-node tests might span different racks. But generally for p4d, cluster PG is recommended for consistent latency.

[20:30] Vanessa (Redwood): Okay.

[20:32] Priya K. (AWS Networking): Also ensure that the security group rules are symmetrical and wide enough for intra-nodegroup. A lot of people do “allow TCP 443” and forget UDP or ephemeral.

[20:43] Harish (Redwood): Ours is “all traffic within SG,” but I’ll double-check NACL.

[20:49] Megan (AWS TAM): Great.

[20:51] Jamal (Redwood): Anything else you’d recommend for AMI builds to reduce first boot time?

[20:58] Arjun (AWS SA): Disable unattended upgrades, preconfigure container runtime, and ensure time sync is stable. Also consider using SSM parameters or user data as minimal as possible.

[21:10] Sahana (Redwood): We do some of that. Our security hardening adds a few steps, but we can optimize.

[21:18] Derek (AWS EC2 Specialist): For GPU: ensure persistence mode is enabled if you want consistent behavior, but that’s not huge.

[21:25] Vanessa (Redwood): We enable it.

[21:27] (pause)

[21:29] Megan (AWS TAM): Let’s talk about VPC endpoints quickly. Priya, what do you suggest as minimum set for this workload?

[21:37] Priya K. (AWS Networking): For bootstrapping nodes pulling images and artifacts: S3 gateway endpoint, ECR API endpoint, ECR DKR endpoint, STS endpoint, and maybe CloudWatch logs if you’re shipping logs directly. Also if you’re using SSM, then SSM endpoints.

[21:56] Harish (Redwood): We do ship logs, but mostly to our own stack. Still, CloudWatch might be used by the base image.

[22:05] Priya K. (AWS Networking): Even if you don’t, some agents try. If it fails, it can slow down.

[22:11] Gabe (Redwood): That might explain some random delays.

[22:15] Vanessa (Redwood): Ok.

[22:17] Megan (AWS TAM): We’re at about halfway. Any other questions from Redwood?

[22:23] Jamal (Redwood): One more: are there known “first 10 minutes after launch” performance characteristics on p4d that would affect our throughput checks? Like disk warmup or network warmup.

[22:35] Derek (AWS EC2 Specialist): Disk warmup can be a thing if you’re using EBS volumes that haven’t been initialized, but p4d has instance store too. If you’re attaching new EBS and doing lots of writes, the first time can be slower.

[22:49] Gabe (Redwood): We format and mount. We might be doing filesystem operations before the tests.

[22:56] Arjun (AWS SA): You can pre-warm by reading the volume. But again, best is to keep it consistent.

[23:04] Vanessa (Redwood): Noted.

[23:06] (small crosstalk)

[23:09] Megan (AWS TAM): Okay. I’ll propose a plan: you send logs for one or two recent failures, we review and see if there’s a common AWS factor. Meanwhile you run two experiments: (1) enable endpoints, (2) bring-up with EFA disabled, and compare.

[23:25] Vanessa (Redwood): That matches what we want.

[23:28] Jamal (Redwood): And we’ll check IMDS hop limit.

[23:32] Arjun (AWS SA): I’ll send guidance. Also, if you’re using Calico or Cilium, the IMDS iptables rules matter.

[23:42] Gabe (Redwood): We use Cilium.

[23:44] Arjun (AWS SA): Yeah, then pay attention to host firewall settings.

[23:49] Sahana (Redwood): That’s likely relevant.

[23:52] Priya K. (AWS Networking): Cilium sometimes adjusts routes early and can impact access to link-local addresses like IMDS.

[24:01] Vanessa (Redwood): Great catch.

[24:04] Megan (AWS TAM): Okay. Do you need anything from AWS besides the docs and checks?

[24:10] Jamal (Redwood): If you can check whether there are any regional advisories or known issues for p4d bring-up in us-east, that would be helpful.

[24:19] Derek (AWS EC2 Specialist): I can look for host advisories and known patterns. But I’ll need instance IDs if we want to go deeper.

[24:27] Gabe (Redwood): We’ll provide.

[24:29] Megan (AWS TAM): Perfect.

[24:31] (transcription skips ahead slightly)

[24:33] Vanessa (Redwood): One more thing: sometimes the validation fails because it can’t pull the perf canary image. That seems like ECR auth. Would STS endpoint fix that?
